prize_parts.citation: for transparent, credibly identified evidence on how technology and import competition reshape labour demand, wages and local labour-market adjustment

statement.case_for: B032 combines a conceptual framework (tasks and technology) with transparent quasi-experimental designs on import competition. The work has been scrutinised for 10 to 20 years by many independent groups, has been re-examined under alternative specifications, and has shaped policy debate on globalisation and automation. Its central qualitative findings, that local labour markets adjust slowly and that exposed workers bear persistent costs, have survived this scrutiny, even though the magnitudes are still debated. I value that record of open, exposed-to-criticism empirical work. I have moved from my opening two names to three. Several colleagues stressed that Dorn is a core co-author of the China-shock design, and a trio of Autor, Dorn and Hanson tracks the identifiable credit line for the evidence better than a pair does. The three-name ceiling then leaves no room for a second part, so I propose a single-achievement prize rather than dilute attribution.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. The task-based framework draws on contributors who are not in this credited set, notably Levy and Murnane and Acemoglu and Restrepo, and Acemoglu was recognised in 2024. Katz's work on the skill premium is also left out of my trio. Separately, the aggregate magnitude and long-run persistence of the China-shock effects, and the inference properties of exposure-based (shift-share) designs, remain contested. The prize would honour robust local-labour-market evidence rather than a settled aggregate number.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B032 first but with Katz instead of Dorn. She stresses that omitting Dorn from a three-person cap is a real attribution judgement call, and she notes overlap with recent labour-market recognition (Goldin, Card).
responses.response: I agree that omitting Dorn is the costliest exclusion, which is why I moved to include him. I weigh Katz differently. His skill-premium work is foundational, but it is a separate, earlier contribution from the trade-shock design. The citation I propose is about identification of technology and trade effects on local labour demand, and Autor, Dorn and Hanson share that line most closely. If the Committee wants the broader skill-and-technology narrative, Katz's claim becomes stronger, but then I would want the citation to say so explicitly. I do not think the Goldin and Card overlap is serious. Their prizes concerned gender gaps and minimum-wage and immigration natural experiments, not trade and technology shocks to labour demand.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B010 first and B032 second. She notes that the task-model attribution is incomplete without Acemoglu and Restrepo, and that long-run effects and exposure-design identification are still debated.
responses.response: I share the attribution worry, and it is the main reason I frame the citation around empirical evidence on labour demand and local adjustment instead of the task theory. That framing fits the credited names. The identification debate matters to me as a metascience concern, but my recollection is that the exposure designs have been reanalysed with alternative inference and specifications and the core local effects have held up. The aggregate magnitude has not. I would rank B010 below B032 because the firm-heterogeneity model's quantitative welfare gains depend more on functional-form choices, such as the Pareto assumption, than the transparent reduced-form designs do. I accept that this is a judgement and not a decisive scientific difference.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B016 first. He argues that Persson and Tabellini built modern political economics, and that the 2024 institutions prize covered adjacent but distinct ground.
responses.response: I agree that B016 created a field and I rank it third. My hesitation is about credibility of evidence rather than importance. Parts of the cross-country constitutional evidence rest on observational variation, and I hold that more strictly than the quasi-experimental local designs in B032. I also see a more material thematic overlap with the 2024 prize than you do. A committee can reasonably weigh this either way, so I keep B016 outside my two named alternatives. I would not oppose a B016 prize on scientific grounds if the identification caveats were reflected in the citation.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B014 first. He says the framework shaped central-bank practice, that the post-2021 inflation did not undermine the core contributions, and that the timing is arguably overdue.
responses.response: I agree that B014's practical influence is very large, and it is my second choice. I would qualify two points. First, the framework's predictive performance after 2008 and in 2021 to 2023 deserves weight, since much of its empirical content is model-dependent. Second, attribution is the hard problem. With eight credited names and at least five distinct contributions, any trio will be contested, and that costs the prize some legitimacy. I take your point that Calvo, Taylor and Woodford is the most defensible conceptual cut. I still prefer B032 because its credit line is tighter and its core findings are more directly checkable against data. I am open to B014 if the Committee converges on that trio.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B042 first and argues that Kiyotaki and Moore's 1997 paper is a clean joint contribution, with Gertler and Gilchrist belonging to an adjacent accelerator strand tied to Bernanke.
responses.response: I accept that attribution for B042 is the cleanest on the list and that the mechanism is foundational. That is why it is one of my two alternatives. My reservation is about empirical grounding. The collateral channel is better established as theory than as an identified causal effect, and the overlap with the 2022 prize is real, though that prize addressed bank runs and banking and not collateral-constraint amplification. I rank it fourth because of this gap between theoretical and empirical standing. I would not oppose it, and a Kiyotaki and Moore two-person prize would also fit within the three-name limit.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats the task framework and the trade-shock evidence as one achievement, and whether Katz should replace Dorn or Hanson.

The long-run persistence and aggregate size of the China-shock effects, and how far exposure-based designs withstand alternative inference methods; my knowledge of the latest re-examinations is incomplete.
How much credit for the task framework lies with contributors outside the credited names (Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu, Restrepo), and how that interacts with the 2024 prize.
Whether the Committee would prefer B014 despite its diffuse attribution, or B042 for its cleaner two-person credit.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. None of the candidates in my preferred configuration or named alternatives appears among her listed co-authors, collaborators or institutional ties. Her connections to former committee members and to the Institute for Replication network involve people who are not shortlisted candidates.
